Press Release:


Honeymoon Murder Week 5
Is Shrien Dewani the mastermind behind Anni Hindocha's death? This week’s developments included state witness Zola Tongo, the taxi driver convicted for Anni’s murder, remaining in the hot seat as his cross-examination continued for six days. Carte Blanche analyses the so-called Honeymoon Murder trial, now in its fifth week.


Script:


DEWANI SCRIPT WEEK FIVE

John Webb:
Dramatic CCTV footage was released this week showing Shrien Dewani just after hearing that his wife’s body had been found. Also of Anni’s distraught father, Vinod Hindocha. Opposite him is his son-in-law. Was Shrien Dewani behind Anni’s murder or were the four co-conspirators acting alone?

Week Five. The High Court vicinity remains a hive of activity. Nearby coffee shops are doing a great trade, office workers and photographers still assemble to see Dewani being brought to court. Police also have their hands full trying to contain pop-up protests relating to other matters to make sure they don’t block the families arriving.

These high-profile cases always attract a band of regular court watchers.

Court Watcher #1:
What actually initiated it was the Oscar case. I was absolutely glued to the TV.

Court Watcher #2:
I hope that the truth does come out for their sakes.

John Webb:
They’ll have spent most of this week watching the grueling cross-examination of one of the State’s main witnesses, taxi driver Zola Tongo by Defense Advocate Francois Van Zyl. Tongo, who struck a plea bargain with the State, said that Dewani hired him to organize the hijacking and murder of his wife.

Right up front, Dewani’s defense asked Tongo why he would become involved in such criminality.

Defense Advocate Van Zyl asked Tongo how much he could earn in a good month: between 30 and 40 thousand rand was the taxi driver’s response. Van Zyl then asked how it was possible that he would be prepared to sacrifice his livelihood and his car for a mere R5,000 fee.

Taxi drivers with a permit to operate at Cape Town International Airport have to wait in queues until it’s their chance to pick up travelers. Zola Tongo was someone known as a tout, who operated illegally with no permit. Touts don’t wait in queues; they simply park in the free 30-minute pickup-and-go parkade and as you see here, approach travelers and offer their services, much to the dismay of legal taxi drivers.

Taxi Driver:
That Tonga is in and out. All the touters they are just in and out at the airport. Not doing the queue. If he get a person now, within one hour he can get two to three people.

John Webb:
Once a touter has established a relationship with travelers, they can provide shuttling services. For example, Tongo charged the Dewanis more than R1,000 for an evening trip.

Interview:
These guys, like Mr. Tonga, they can charge any amount. That’s why- because they’re accountable to nobody. That’s why they can take care and maybe get away with it.

John Webb:
And make a lot of money! Tongo in court said that he went ahead with the hijacking because Dewani promised him future work.

The defense spent a great deal of time highlighting inconsistencies between what Zola Tongo had told the court in this trial and what he had told the police immediately after his arrest. It was during this process that major gaps started appearing in his version.

Tongo explained these inconsistencies by saying, “As time goes on, I can just remember some of the things. Some of the things are resurfacing.”

But the defense’s biggest bombshell came towards the end of Zola Tongo’s cross-examination. Advocate Francois Van Zyl says he intends calling, as a witness, an inmate from the same prison in which Zola Tongo was being held. That witness, Bernard Mitchell, will bring startling revelations to Court.

For example, that Tongo, who struck a plea bargain with the State, admitted to him that he was glad that he did not get a life sentence for Anni’s murder. The plan was to kidnap Anni and hold it to ransom. But one of the men involved tried to rape her. There was a struggle and she was shot accidentally. Tongo rejected the defense’s account, saying this was “nonsense and lies” and concocted by someone “who saw this on TV.”

Last week the court was shown CCTV footage of the morning after the hijacking. Tongo said in court that Dewani had repeatedly approached him, asking if there was any news. He said that he warned Dewani that there were cameras overhead. Here it appears that Dewani looks up towards the camera.

The Defense didn’t challenge Tongo about this particular sequence, but this week when police officer Vinesh Lutchman took the stand, he testified about a phone call he received from Tongo. In this footage, captured a few days after Anni’s body was found, you can see Dewani asking to speak to Tongo. He moves away from the group. The State felt that this was suspicious behavior but the defense brushed it off, saying he was just being polite.

There was more drama to follow when Monde Mbolombo, seen here, besieged by photographers, came to the stand. He is the so-called middleman who put Tongo in connection with the hit men. He received indemnity from prosecution for his role in the crime.

Monde Mbolombo took to the stand and immediately made an astonishing admission. He said that he lied in his original police statement, he lied in his 204 statement, and he lied in the trial of Xolile Mgeni. This time around though, he said he’s going to tell the truth.

Defense Attorney William Booth finds this quite odd.

William Booth:
Well it is a bit unusual, you know it’s not every day that a witness comes and says, look I lied on these previous occasions. But, I mean, then again, can you believe what he’s now going to tell the court if he’s lied before?

John Webb:
Perhaps not too surprised by Mbolombo’s confession is British-born journalist, Dan Newling, who now lives in South Africa. He arrived in the country just before Anni’s murder. He was the first person to interview Dewani after his wife’s death.

Dan Newling:
He was obviously traumatized. He told me he hadn’t slept for 56 hours, which is a rather long time, and he appeared a little bit confused.

John:
Dan Newling has written a controversial book called Bitter Dawn: A Search for the Truth about the Murder of Anni Dewani. Prior to the trial, many people felt that Dewani was guilty. But he believes that he’s put forward compelling reasons to challenge the establishment story.

Dan Newling:
I’m careful in the book not to come to any strong conclusion or any personal conclusion, but it’s clear from the trial here and from my research, there are rather strong questions for the State, for the NPA, for the police.

John:
He questions the ease with which criminals can cut plea bargains with the State and reminds readers of the high South Africa was on after hosting the soccer World Cup in 2010. Anni’s murder happened just a few months after the event.

Dan Newling:
You just had the World Cup, it was a wonderful success. You defy the world’s expectations. Bheki Cele was crowing from the roofs about the success of that tournament, and then all of a sudden, this happens, and as Bheki Cele tells me in the final chapter of my book, he tells me that this was something that ruined the country’s otherwise improving reputation.

John:
It seems that following the performances of some of the State’s witnesses in this trial that questions are starting to emerge. Is it conceivable that the police were perhaps too eager to pin the murder on Shrien Dewani? That is something that has not gone unnoticed by court watchers.

Court Watcher #3:
I found this guy actually guilty before the trial even started when you read the newspapers and stuff, and now I’m having my doubts if this guy is actually guilty.

John:
Where to from here for the State? What more can they do, do you think?

William Booth:
Well I don’t think they can do anymore, unless someone jumps out of the woodwork, which I don’t believe is going to be the case. Realistically, this case rests on the evidence of Qwabe, Tongo, and to a lesser extent, Mbolombo, and they don’t’ seem to be faring very well.

John:
An so another week comes to an end in the Dewani trial with the State witness being grilled by the defense. Mbolombo will be back in the stand on Monday morning
